title: Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit by Dec. 11: Reports
description: US President Donald Trump during an executive order (EO) signing in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026
body: US President Donald Trump during an executive order (EO) signing in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. The executive order will establish a women's health office at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Photographer: Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesAaron Schwartz | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesA federal judge in Miami on Thursday ordered that President Donald Trump sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11, according to multiple news outlets.U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, at a court hearing Thursday, also warned Trump's attorneys that if the president does not comply with court orders to give lawyers for the British media outlet records that are relevant to the lawsuit, his complaint could be dismissed, Politico reported.  Trump's lawyers had requested that his deposition be conducted between Jan. 11 and Jan. 22.This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

schema.headline: Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit by Dec. 11: Reports

title: Pepsi renews contract with Taco Bell days after KFC switches to Coke in the U.S.
description: A staff member is seen at a Taco Bell restaurant in London.May James | Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesPepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their lon
body: A staff member is seen at a Taco Bell restaurant in London.May James | Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesPepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their long-running partnership through 2036, the food and beverage company said on Thursday.The announcement comes one week after Taco Bell's sister chain KFC said that it will switch to Coca-Cola as its U.S. beverage supplier. While it is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch drink providers, the move is not unprecedented, as Coke and Pepsi try to win contracts through perks and other inducements. Coke's win over Pepsi was more symbolic, representing another example of how the Atlanta-based company has been beating its rival in the soda category.Pepsi's relationship with Taco Bell and KFC parent Yum Brands spans decades, back to when the beverage giant owned the restaurant chains before spinning them into a separate public company in 1997. Despite KFC's defection in the U.S., Pepsi remains an important partner for Yum and the chain's international markets, KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo on Oct. 15 that was obtained by CNBC. Thanks to its partnership with Pepsi, Taco Bell has long served exclusive menu items that use Pepsi products, like Mountain Dew Baja Blast and Doritos Locos Tacos, at its restaurants.The renewed deal also means that Taco Bell international markets such as Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Thailand will serve Pepsi products.

schema.headline: Pepsi renews contract with Taco Bell days after KFC switches to Coke in the U.S.

title: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues
description: A job seeker holds paperwork during the Mega JobNewsUSA South Florida Job Fair held in the Amerant Bank Arena on Sept. 25, 2026 in Sunrise, Florida. J
body: A job seeker holds paperwork during the Mega JobNewsUSA South Florida Job Fair held in the Amerant Bank Arena on Sept. 25, 2026 in Sunrise, Florida. Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesEmployers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ending Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29. Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period."Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The September jobs report will be released Nov. 5.Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue their latest decision on interest rates. Policymakers in recent days have characterized the labor market as a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesome inflation problem that has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.

schema.headline: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues

title: American Express brings Airbnb bookings and rewards to Amex Travel platform
description: Adamdodd | GettyAmerican Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform. The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring m
body: Adamdodd | GettyAmerican Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform. The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring more than 1 million Airbnb listings to Amex's travel portal and allow cardholders to earn rewards when booking the stays. It does not currently allow members to redeem points to pay for Airbnb bookings.The launch adds Airbnb rentals to Amex's hotel portfolio, which includes more than 3,400 properties across its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs. Amex members with either the consumer or business Platinum card can also now apply their $600 annual lodging credit — previously called the hotel credit — to Airbnb's higher-end Luxe stays and take advantage of a new $250 statement credit on eligible Airbnb Experiences after making a Luxe booking. "We're excited to bring more choice and flexibility to American Express Card Members with this exclusive partnership. Both of our companies exist to help people travel more and better, and this partnership helps people see more of the world by making travel more rewarding," said Juan David Borrero, head of partnerships at Airbnb, in a news release. Membership points vary by card: Consumer and Business Platinum Card members earn five times the membership rewards on prepaid Airbnb bookings through Amex Travel. Consumer Classic Green Card members earn three times the points on travel bookings made directly through third-party sites, including Airbnb. Other eligible rewards members earn two times the points on prepaid Airbnb bookings through Amex Travel.The changes come as competition among premium credit cards continues to ramp up. Last year, American Express raised the annual fee on its premium Platinum card to $895. In turn, it's been investing in cardholder perks such as new lounges in airports and at big-ticket events and experiences as a way to attract more high-paying customers. Earlier this month, it announced an expansion of its Centurion Lounges, with renovations coming to four existing lounges and new ones planned for Newark Liberty International Airport and London Heathrow Airport. The Newark lounge will be the largest in its network.The partnership also comes as Americans continue to opt for travel and luxury experiences, even as prices for airfare, gas and hotels rise. Despite higher costs, more than half of Americans reported making no changes to their travel plans this summer, a recent study by travel insurance company Squaremouth found.

schema.headline: American Express brings Airbnb bookings and rewards to Amex Travel platform

title: World's largest wealth fund posts $30 billion loss after bond market turbulence
description: Nicolai Tangen, chief executive officer of NBIM, at the Norges Bank Climate Conference in Oslo, Norway, on Oct. 21, 2025.Naina Helén Jåma | Bloomberg
body: Nicolai Tangen, chief executive officer of NBIM, at the Norges Bank Climate Conference in Oslo, Norway, on Oct. 21, 2025.Naina Helén Jåma | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNorway's sovereign wealth fund — the largest in the world — said Thursday that its investment portfolio delivered a loss of $30 billion in the third quarter, as rising interest rates dented returns on its bond holdings. Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages the $2.3 trillion fund, said the accounting return for the period was a loss of 278 billion kroner ($29.7 billion). Around 70% of NBIM's fixed income portfolio is allocated to government bonds, with the remainder invested in corporate debt.The third quarter saw a global bond market rout. Government bond yields surged as major central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve, began rate-hiking cycles and concerns about inflation and government debt levels mounted. NBIM's fixed income investments delivered a negative return of 3.5%, with the fund's management saying this was a key driver of the overall downturn. "The fund's return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments," NBIM's Deputy CEO Trond Grande said in a statement. Fixed income accounts for just over a quarter of the fund's entire portfolio, with NBIM invested in 1,664 bonds across 51 countries.Last month, NBIM said it wanted to cut its U.S. Treasury holdings as part of wider plans to reduce its allocation to government-issued debt.Equities, which account for 72% of the sovereign wealth fund's investments, returned 0.5% for the fund in the third quarter. The fund has small stakes in around 7,100 companies across most countries. With holdings in 1.5% of all listed companies globally, it is the world's largest single investor. Stock markets were turbulent in the three months to September. Wall Street's major averages ended the third quarter in mixed territory. The S&P 500 index added 2.03%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended the quarter 2.2% higher.The average change across the three indexes was just 0.6%, marking a slowdown in the rally that saw double-digit gains in the previous quarter.NBIM is an investor in America's biggest companies, with its top holdings including a $65.4 billion stake in Nvidia, as well as positions in Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft. Its positions in the world's biggest companies make NBIM influential in terms of both voting power and setting investment trends. "Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell," Grande said Thursday. Energy stocks benefited from surging oil prices in the third quarter, as the U.S.-Iran war continued, said NBIM, which has stakes in various energy majors, including Exxon Mobil, Shell and Chevron. Over the summer, NBIM CEO Nicolai Tangen told CNBC that investors should not expect a continuation of the bumper gains seen in the stock market in the first half of this year."For sure, we should not be expecting the same kind of returns going forward as we've seen over the last six months," he said at the time. The fund delivered a first-half return of 12.95%, and a record first-half profit nearing $185 billion. It also invests in real estate and renewable energy infrastructure, which returned 0.4% and 7.5%, respectively, in the third quarter. Norway established its sovereign wealth fund in 1998 to invest revenues from the country's oil.

schema.headline: World's largest wealth fund posts $30 billion loss after bond market turbulence

title: Blackstone's Jon Gray says CoreWeave can 'find a way through' financing pressure
description: CoreWeave has been battered over concerns about its massive debt, but Blackstone chief operating officer Jon Gray believes the so-called neocloud comp
body: CoreWeave has been battered over concerns about its massive debt, but Blackstone chief operating officer Jon Gray believes the so-called neocloud company will weather the storm. Right now, CoreWeave and its neocloud peers are facing challenges over the capital needed to deliver on their promises, he said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box" Thursday."Some of these companies have very talented CEOs. CoreWeave is a good example of this," Gray said. "They'll find a way through it, but that's the challenge they face. The underlying business is actually quite strong."CoreWeave has seen its stock sink, bond yields rise and spreads on its credit default swaps widen over the past week as investors became nervous about how the company will continue to finance its data centers, and at what cost. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreweave's one-month performanceDemand for computing power, however, is strong, said Gray. He is seeing that across the board in the private companies the firm holds. At the same time, there is a constraint in delivering supply, he said. "For the neo clouds, if they can get to the other side, the pricing of compute is up 50%," he said. "Their legacy chips are worth much more than people thought. Their data centers are leased below market."Shares of CoreWeave sank 3.55% on Thursday, and are down 14% over the past week. Blackstone earningsGray spoke with CNBC after Blackstone reported its third-quarter results, which came in mixed. Its stock was up 4% on Thursday. Blackstone saw quarterly revenue of $3.22 billion, short of the $3.28 billion expected from analysts polled by LSEG. Its adjusted earnings of $1.32 per share, however, topped the $1.26 consensus estimate. It was a "challenging quarter with markets" thanks to high energy prices and the rise in Treasury yields, Gray said. However, the firm delivered for its clients, he noted. "Across the board, our flagship strategies beat comparable public market indices and that's what we care most about," he said. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBlackstone year to dateHe anticipates a strong fourth quarter and 2027, despite some cross-currents like the rising cost of capital, government deficits and some crowding out of capital due to the AI infrastructure build. However, good news is there is underlying economic and earnings strength, he said. Gray also expects initial public offerings to resume once the market and geopolitical situation calms a bit. He said investors just need to have some patience."We have a long-term approach, and we feel very good about where we position capital for our investors, the growth of those companies, the growth of those assets, and that's what gives us confidence," he said. "At some point, the wider window will open, and when that happens, we and others will sell even more."

schema.headline: Blackstone's Jon Gray says CoreWeave can 'find a way through' financing pressure

title: Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case
description: Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, listens during a reconvened legislative session to vote on Gov. Abigail Spanberger's amendments to the Virginia budge
body: Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, listens during a reconvened legislative session to vote on Gov. Abigail Spanberger's amendments to the Virginia budget, Monday, June 29, 2026 at the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond, Va. (Mike Kropf/Richmond Times-Dispatch via Getty Images)Mike Kropf | Richmond Times-dispatch | Getty ImagesVirginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas has been charged in a federal indictment with leading an alleged marijuana racketeering conspiracy that included family members of the powerful Democrat, according to court documents made public on Thursday.Lucas, 82, is a critic of President Donald Trump, and was an architect of ultimately failed efforts in Virginia to redraw the state's congressional map for November to boost chances for Democrats to win those districts.The criminal case, which also charges members of Lucas' family, was made public by the Department of Justice less than two weeks before the midterm elections. Those contests will determine what political party controls both chambers of Congress.Lucas, the state Senate's president pro tempore and chairman of the Finance and Appropriations Committee, is not on the ballot this year. She was elected to the Senate in 1991.The indictment says that Lucas "was the leader of the enterprise," that she "arranged for the acquisition and distribution of marijuana, supervises the laundering of marijuana proceeds," and "used her political influence to attempt to influence Virginia legislation for the benefit of herself and her family and maintained a premise for the distribution of marijuana."Six other defendants are charged in the alleged scheme, among them Lucas' two daughters and her grandson. One of the daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke, is running for mayor of Portsmouth. Lucas is in custody with the other defendants, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced at a press conference Thursday. She is scheduled to appear before a magistrate judge in U.S. District Court in Norfolk, Virginia, at 2:30 p.m. ET Thursday."Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother," Lucas said in a statement posted on X."I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now," she said. "I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down." Blanche, when asked at the press conference about criticism from Lucas's attorney that the case is politically motivated, said, "We don't do political paybacks." The attorney general noted that the investigation of Lucas began before the current Trump administration, and that a federal grand jury had determined there was enough evidence to indict her."There's decision and processes in place at the department when we're bringing a case against a political official, and the ... first question is: is this investigation proper?" Blanche said. "And the conclusion of that is yes.  Is the timing proper? And the conclusion of that is yes."The indictment was issued by a grand jury on Oct. 14, but was only unsealed Thursday.The charges come five months after FBI agents executed a search warrant at Lucas' Portsmouth office.At the time of that May 6 raid, Lucas noted in a statement that it came two weeks after Virginia voters approved the redistricting plan, adding, "Virginians sent a powerful message when they voted to stop Trump's scheme to manipulate the 2026 midterm elections.""I was proud to help lead that effort and I have never been afraid to stand up to Donald Trump."

schema.headline: Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case

title: Procter & Gamble earnings beat as sales rise 4%, boosted by laundry and home products
description: Procter & Gamble on Thursday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations, fueled by growing demand for its laundry deterg
body: Procter & Gamble on Thursday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations, fueled by growing demand for its laundry detergent and home care products.Shares of the company rose more than 5% in morning trading.Here's what the company reported for the three-month period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $2.00 adjusted vs. $1.88 expectedRevenue: $23.3 billion vs. $22.8 billion expectedP&G reported fiscal first-quarter net income attributable to the company of $4.73 billion, or $1.97 per share, down from $4.75 billion, or $1.95 per share, a year earlier.Excluding restructuring costs and other items, the company earned $2 per share.Net sales rose 4% to $23.3 billion.Bottles of Dawn dish spray are displayed for sale at a Target store on August 4, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesP&G reported volume growth of 2.4%, a strong start for its new fiscal year. Like many consumer companies, P&G has seen demand for its products weaken as shoppers have become more value-conscious.  Executives have previously said that consumers are now using every last drop of shampoo or laundry detergent, and value packs have become more popular. In fiscal 2026, P&G reported just one quarter of volume growth. P&G is still seeing signs of a bifurcated economy, CFO Andre Schulten said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday. High-income consumers are willing to trade up to new products, even a $30 shampoo, while low-income consumers are trying to make brands like Tide and Pampers work for their tight budgets. The company has tried to address both ends of the spectrum with promotional pricing, new pack sizes and product innovation that can command higher prices. New premium products like Pampers Amore and Pantene's Abundant & Strong haircare line have helped P&G grow market share in those categories, executives said.Adding to P&G's challenges, the competitive environment is "intense," Schulten said on the company's quarterly earnings call."We are getting the balance between pricing and product improvements, package improvements, claims, communication and retail execution right," Schulten told analysts. "But it's also a very fragile balance that we want to make sure we we don't compromise on, so we will price, and we will price with innovation, not jeopardizing the top-line momentum."P&G's top-performing division was fabric and home care, which includes brands like Tide and Febreze. The segment's volume rose 4.3% in the quarter, helped by stronger demand for laundry detergent and fabric enhancers.The company's baby, feminine and family care segment and its beauty business both reported volume growth of more than 2%.P&G's grooming division saw volume shrink 0.4% in the quarter. The segment includes Gillette and Venus razors.The company's healthcare business was the laggard of the portfolio this quarter. Its volume fell 2.9% as demand for oral healthcare products, like Crest toothpaste, and personal healthcare items, like Pepto-Bismol, shrank.The company is expecting continued "geopolitical and economic challenges," but P&G is on track to meet its guidance, CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said in a statement.For fiscal 2027, P&G reiterated its forecast for core earnings per share in a range of $6.89 to $7.11. The company is now projecting all-in sales growth in the range of 2% to 4% compared with the prior year, up from its previous outlook of 1% to 3%. The change reflects its acquisition of supplements brand Thorne, which closed Oct. 1.

schema.headline: Procter & Gamble earnings beat as sales rise 4%, boosted by laundry and home products

title: France protests: Macron condemns 'stupid' comments from Trump, others as bond market pressure builds
description: France's President Emmanuel Macron speaks to members of the media on the day of the 9th Annual One Planet Sovereign Wealth Funds (OPSWF) Summit in Lus
body: France's President Emmanuel Macron speaks to members of the media on the day of the 9th Annual One Planet Sovereign Wealth Funds (OPSWF) Summit in Lusail on October 21, 2026. Benoit Tessier | Afp | Getty ImagesFrench President Emmanuel Macron has criticized "unacceptable" and "stupid" comments made by foreign leaders and others after the country saw mass protests and its worst rioting in years. "There was foreign disinformation in the aftermath, which prompted comments that were as unacceptable as they were stupid from many people, including foreign leaders," Macron told reporters Wednesday, according to Reuters. Macron clarified he was talking about U.S. President Donald Trump "among others," and said politicians were using the situation in France for their own ends. Posting on his Truth social platform, Trump earlier this week blamed the unrest on "migrants, jihadists, and Communists" and told Europe to close its borders. Trump and other Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance and House Speaker Mike Johnson, have referenced the unrest in France on the campaign trail ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterms. They have claimed that Democrat policies on immigration would raise similar tensions. Political sparring has extended to government agencies. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, wrote on X on Wednesday that it was "fighting to prevent American streets from looking like this." The post included footage that appeared to reference rioters in France.The French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs responded on its own X account that it was "fighting to prevent French stats from looking like this," showing a graphic displaying the gulf in U.S. firearm homicides per 100,000 people over G7 peers.Officials in Iran — where rights groups say authorities killed hundreds of people during a crackdown on recent demonstrations — have also weighed in, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling on Macron to listen to the protesters' demands. Separate protests also took place in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Albania on Saturday and Sunday. Thousands of people marched in Greece on Wednesday for improved education services, in solidarity with French students whose protests were the initial trigger for mounting unrest in the country.  Tensions remain high in France. Student union UNEF and the anti-establishment "gilets jaunes," or "yellow vest" group, have both called for further rallies this coming weekend. Macron — who has faced criticism this week for embarking on a tour of Gulf countries — has vowed that there will be no repeat of the recent violence. Several French cities were rocked by looting and arson at the weekend, alongside mass peaceful protests over the state of public services, the cost of living and discontent with political leadership. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Wednesday that some military forces would be deployed to help maintain order.French bond turmoil worsens French social and political volatility is compounded by an emerging fiscal crisis, which on Thursday pushed its benchmark government borrowing cost to a fresh 24-year high. The yield on 10-year French government bonds soared another 11 basis points later Thursday morning, hitting 5.113% and surpassing the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury for the first time since 2013. Investors are increasingly skeptical that France will pass a program of fiscal consolidation to shrink its high deficit-to-gross domestic product ratio. Parliament is currently debating its 2027 budget, but the government lacks a parliamentary majority and may resort to special powers. Using those powers could provide short-term budget certainty but would likely stoke further political volatility.France is facing spiraling debt servicing payments that are putting further pressure on its finances, raising the specter of potential intervention by the European Central Bank if the spread in its borrowing costs against euro area benchmark Germany continues to widen.Businesses and insurers are meanwhile facing a financial hit from the recent protests, both from direct costs and public perception around the country.Morningstar has estimated the cost of insured losses at up to 1.2 billion euros ($1.34 billion) amid widespread theft and damage to commercial premises and public buildings, assuming no further significant impact. "The direct economic impact on France of the unrest surrounding the 17 October protests is likely to be limited, but it comes at a challenging time for the economy and public finances," Mehdi Fadli, senior vice president for global sovereign ratings at Morningstar, told CNBC by email. Fadli noted the government's recent revision of its 2026 real GDP growth forecast to 0.5% from 1%."Against a backdrop of continued uncertainty surrounding the international environment and the domestic presidential election, prolonged protests could further weigh on household and business confidence, dampening economic activity and exacerbating fiscal pressures in both 2026 and 2027," Fadli said.

schema.headline: France protests: Macron condemns 'stupid' comments from Trump, others as bond market pressure builds

title: Meta stock sinks 6% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative
description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wears the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, as he delivers a speech presenting the new line of smart glasses, during the Meta Con
body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wears the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, as he delivers a speech presenting the new line of smart glasses, during the Meta Connect event at the company's headquarters in Menlo Park, California, U.S., Sept. 17, 2025. Carlos Barria | ReutersMeta shares slumped roughly 6% on Thursday as the social media giant showed negative free cash flow in its third-quarter earnings and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditures.The spread on the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs on Thursday, a signal of growing credit concerns from investors as the company leans deeper into its artificial intelligence spending plans. Meta said it expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from a previous $130 billion to $145 billion.Free cash flow came in at a negative $2.12 billion during the quarter.The company revealed Wednesday that it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock during its earnings release, meant to maintain its "founder-led structure" and "provide Meta the ability to finance its growth."Meta also said CEO Mark Zuckerberg could leave the state if the "California Wealth Tax" were to pass, as he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company," according to the SEC filing.Zuckerberg was convinced to stay in California with the company's new stock plan, the filing noted.Revenue for the social media giant jumped 26% in the third quarter from a year ago, coming in at $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share were reported at $3.83, though it wasn't clear if it was directly comparable to the $5.75 per share Wall Street was looking for. —CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and Seema Mody contributed to this report. title: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms
description: An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Sept. 19, 2026.AFP | Getty ImagesThe U.S. ordered non-emergency
body: An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Sept. 19, 2026.AFP | Getty ImagesThe U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalate.The move comes as the U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, according to The New York Times, citing unnamed U.S. officials. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.  The developments point to a possible widening of the nearly eight-month war, while U.S. and Iranian negotiators continue talks on Tehran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz.State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets. Meanwhile, Reuters reported Washington also plans to withdraw family members from other missions in the region.A strike Wednesday on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least one person and injured eight. Two people died in a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field, the Saudi Press Agency reported, adding that operations were not affected.In recent days, the U.S. and Israeli militaries have stepped up military exercises, including flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers, according to The New York Times. The Times also reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel this week to discuss potential new strikes. The renewed military strikes would likely target Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal, according to The Times, noting that President Donald Trump has yet to approve the fresh strikes and has repeatedly vetoed plans for a return to major combat this year. Iranian officials have vowed to widen their attacks to target data centers and undersea internet cables, while refusing concessions on their nuclear program. Despite the persistent shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Middle East oil flows through the vital strait have recovered to near pre‑war levels according to Kpler. As Brent crude topped $110 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate gained 1% to $98.12, recovering appetite for crude from China could drive oil prices higher, according to the commodity research firm.   "China's crude import demand is expected to continue recovering, driven by rising refinery throughput and rapidly declining crude inventories," said Muyu Xu, senior crude oil analyst at Kpler. The war has cut China's oil stockpiles, with the fastest drawndown on record at 1.6 million barrels a day in September, Xu estimated.China still holds 1.1 billion barrels in reserves, about 80 days of refinery needs, Xu said. She added that with virtually all Iranian cargoes outside the U.S. blockade discharged, substantial new crude arrivals in China appear unlikely.Chinese state-owned refiners are likely to have a stronger appetite and greater urgency to secure prompt Middle Eastern barrels as they face higher throughput and inventory-replenishment needs. Independent refiners are also seeking alternatives to Iranian crude, a shift that could limit further downside in the Dubai structure, Xu said.

schema.headline: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms

title: Brent crude tops $111 after Trump hints at action on Iran, U.S. orders staff to leave Saudi Arabia
description: watch nowOil prices climbed Thursday on worries over a possible escalation in the Middle East conflict as the U.S. reportedly plans to resume strikes
body: watch nowOil prices climbed Thursday on worries over a possible escalation in the Middle East conflict as the U.S. reportedly plans to resume strikes against Iran.Brent crude futures rose 2.8% to $111.81 a barrel as of 11:07 a.m. ET after nearly reaching $113 earlier. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude gained 1.7% to $98.83 after breaking $100 earlier.  The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, unnamed U.S. officials told The New York Times. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, the officials said.President Donald Trump subsequently said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran when asked by a reporter late Wednesday. Trump said "something one way or the other" will "happen fairly soon" on Iran without elaborating.  "Most people seem to think it's after the election," Trump said. "We're going to see what happens." The U.S. has also ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, dismissing reports that the U.S. had directed some staff in the wider Gulf region to leave. Pigott pointed to escalating attacks by Iran-allied Houthis on civilian targets in Saudi Arabia as the reason for the order. At least two people were killed and eight injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Saudi Arabia's East Coast Wednesday, according to Saudi state media. Meanwhile, oil giant Saudi Aramco has told staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely, people familiar with the matter told Reuters Thursday. Aramco facilities have repeatedly come under attack by the Houthis. The economic fallout from elevated oil prices, however, may be less severe than in previous decades, as consumers have become less vulnerable to energy shocks, according to David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors."$100 oil today is very different than $100 oil, you know, 20, 30 years ago," Wagner said, noting that crude prices remain well below their inflation-adjusted historical highs.He pointed to U.S. government data showing that gasoline accounted for roughly 5% of the average American's disposable income a decade ago, compared with about half that today, suggesting households may be better positioned to withstand elevated energy costs."I think we can hold that umbrella over our head ... from the rainstorm of oil," he said.— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Brent crude tops $111 after Trump hints at action on Iran, U.S. orders staff to leave Saudi Arabia

title: Southwest Airlines cuts 2026 profit forecast on higher fuel

body: watch nowSouthwest Airlines became the third major U.S. airline this month to cut its 2026 profit forecast due to higher fuel prices, but CEO Bob Jordan said travelers continue to book despite higher fares.The carrier expects to earn between $2.60 and $2.85 a share on an adjusted basis this year, down from its forecast in July of between $3.25 to as much as $4.25 a share.Here's what Southwest reported for third quarter compared with Wall Street expectations, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:Earnings per share: 66 cents adjusted vs. 58 cents expectedRevenue: $8.42 billion adjusted vs. $8.25 billion expectedSouthwest forecast per-share adjusted earnings of between 55 cents and 80 cents in the fourth quarter and unit revenue, a gauge of airfare, up as much as 21% from a year earlier. It said it expects to grow capacity by up to 4% year over year."Demand remained strong as we lapped last year's bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we've built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs," Jordan said in an earnings release.The airline said its average passenger fare was $231.69 in the third quarter, up almost 27% from the same quarter of 2025. A spokesman said that number does not include add-on fees. The number of revenue passengers carried fell 3.2% to 33.47 million people.But Jordan told CNBC's Phil LeBeau that demand was strong across every geography and product."The consumer is incredibly strong and we do not see that abating," Jordan said. "We're seeing strength in both the holiday period and the non-holiday period."Under pressure to grow revenue, Southwest has been remaking its longtime business model over the past several years, scrapping its old policies like two free checked bags per passenger and open seating. In its place, Southwest has started charging for many seat assignments and added a bag fee, similar to major competitors.For the third quarter, Southwest posted net income of $270 million, or 55 cents a share, up from $54 million or 10 cents a share a year earlier. Revenue rose more than 21% to $8.42 billion.Adjusting for one-time items, Southwest reported 66 cents a share.Delta Air Lines and United Airlines also cut their profit outlooks for the rest of the year when they reported third-quarter earnings. title: Spain accuses Trump ally Milei of ‘disgraceful’ election interference
description: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez gestures during a press conference at the Moncloa Palace in Madrid on December 15, 2025.Thomas Coex | Afp | Getty
body: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez gestures during a press conference at the Moncloa Palace in Madrid on December 15, 2025.Thomas Coex | Afp | Getty ImagesSpain's government has become embroiled in a dispute with Argentinian President Javier Milei after the latter accused Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of being a "dictator" while endorsing his right-wing political rivals. Speaking at an event in Madrid on Wednesday, Milei claimed that Spain "suffers [with socialism] under the disgraceful dictator Pedro Sanchez," and urged voters to "kick the socialists out, because you are the cradle of liberalism."The Spanish Foreign Ministry issued a statement condemning Milei's comments — made during an unofficial visit to Spain — as "insults and slander" directed at the country, its prime minister and its population. "Spain is a sovereign nation that does not accept external interference, nor attacks or insults against its Prime Minister and its freely, democratically and sovereignly elected institutions, nor does it tolerate anyone disrupting our peaceful and democratic coexistence," the government said. "It is disgraceful that a person holding the highest office in a sister nation should visit our country with the sole aim of attempting to foster a climate of polarization and violence amongst Spaniards and between sister nations such as Spain and Argentina."Milei's unofficial visit to the Spanish capital on Wednesday comes as Spain gears up for a general election on Nov. 29. Sanchez is the leader of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party and has been Spain's prime minister since 2018. On Oct. 5, Sanchez called an early election after lawmakers voted against housing reforms drawn up in the wake of nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis.  Demonstrators gather in Madrid's city center during a housing rights demonstration outside Madrid City Hall in Madrid, Spain, on October 3, 2026, calling for an end to evictions and greater protection for tenants following the eviction of Maricarmen. Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesHe is running to win a third term in the Nov. 29 snap election — but polls point to a right-wing coalition between the conservative People's Party and far-right Vox being the most likely outcome.The Spanish prime minister has already faced off against Milei, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, in the past. Madrid withdrew its ambassador from Buenos Aires for several months in 2024 after Milei called Sanchez's wife "corrupt" and went on to aim a barrage of insults at Sanchez. Milei publicly criticized Sanchez's government again in June 2025 and September 2026. Milei himself is facing an election in 2027, when he will fight to defend his position against a backdrop of mounting debt problems and a sluggish economy. Sanchez defended his political agenda in a video posted to social media on Wednesday."Some people think they're insulting us when they call us left-wing," he told followers. "Well, let me tell you something: if raising pensions makes me a left-winger, then I'm a left-winger. If giving mothers and fathers more time to enjoy their children makes me left-wing, then I'm left-wing too. If raising the minimum wage every year is a left-wing thing, then I'm left-wing. If defending women's right to abortion makes me left-wing, I am. If standing against war and supporting peace makes me left-wing, I am. So yes, I'm a leftie — and proud of it."Sanchez has also locked horns with Trump this year, with the U.S. president threatening to cut off trade and relations with Spain after the pair traded criticisms over the U.S.-Iran war and defense spending. watch now

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says neocloud demand is 'off the charts' but capital is scarce
description: watch nowNvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neocloud firms is "off the charts," but scarce capital is holding back growth."If
body: watch nowNvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neocloud firms is "off the charts," but scarce capital is holding back growth."If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neo clouds is off the charts," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company's GTC conference in Berlin on Thursday, adding that capabilities are "extraordinary.""What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth… because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital," Huang said."The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital. That's going to get solved," he added.Power is a major constraint for the AI boom, particularly in Europe, where electricity prices are higher. Huang said that the allocation of energy — which is scarce in the region — to companies like Nebius and Mistral is crucial for their growth."You can bring investments into Europe, but you have to start with having your own infrastructure," Huang explained. "If the neoclouds in Europe are able to establish an infrastructure here, then you can build the AI ecosystem, the AI economy on top of them, and then the flywheel of the AI economy will start in Europe. It will terminate in Europe."He added: "Across all of Europe, you're going to need a lot more neoclouds." Neoclouds under pressureNeocloud stocks such as CoreWeave and Nebius have been selling off recently as concerns grow over how much companies are spending on the AI infrastructure buildout, with the return on investments set to take longer than expected. Investors are also wary of how much debt CoreWeave, one of the biggest neocloud players, is using to fund its data center buildout. Neocloud stocks were lower in premarket trading on Thursday, with Nebius down 3.6%, and CoreWeave 4% lower. Iren and Applied Digital also shed nearly 4%. Huang has been on a European media blitz this month as the chip giant looks to expand investments in the region's AI sector. The company has committed nearly $10 billion towards companies, universities, and research institutions. While visiting London last week, Nvidia announced a stake worth over $1 billion in five U.K. startups. The chip giant is also investing in various French startups. "We're trying to kickstart the AI economy in Europe," Huang told CNBC. "Europe has a tremendous amount of technology, tremendous amount of industrial know-how, incredible science and technology, and it's ready to engage and build the AI economy here."

schema.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says neocloud demand is 'off the charts' but capital is scarce
